h1:
Wat Muang, Ang Thong
Thailand's Tallest Buddha
intro: Mention Ang Thong and most people picture Wat Muang first, because the golden Buddha here stands almost 95 metres tall in the middle of open rice fields, visible long before you reach the temple gate. This is Luang Pho Yai, the largest seated Buddha image in Thailand. Around it you'll also find a Hell-Heaven garden, a giant lotus, a glass shrine and a fish pond, all in one temple, all free to enter, and only about two hours from Bangkok. We've pulled together everything you need: what to see, opening hours, and how to get there.

blocks.html: Wat Muang sits in Hua Taphan sub-district, Wiset Chai Chan, about 8 km west of Ang Thong town along Highway 3195 (the Ang Thong–Wiset Chai Chan road). What puts this temple on the map is the giant Buddha you can spot from far away, but once you actually walk in you'll find there's a lot more to see than you'd expect. Whether you're here to make merit, to take photos, or to bring the kids to see the lessons of sin and reward, everyone finds their own way to enjoy a walk around.

blocks.text: Luang Pho Yai — Thailand's largest seated Buddha

blocks.html: The great Buddha's full name is Phra Phuttha Maha Nawamin Sakayamuni Si Wiset Chai Chan. It's a golden Buddha in the bhumisparsha (calling-the-earth-to-witness) posture, with a lap width of around 63 metres and a height of around 95 metres, set out in the open. It took more than a decade to complete. Standing as tall as a high-rise building, the image towers over the rice fields around the temple, and many people see it from the road several kilometres before reaching the entrance.

You can walk in beneath the base of the image to pay your respects. This is a popular photo spot, because if you step back far enough to fit the whole Buddha in frame, you get a shot that really shows the sheer scale. Early morning, before the sun gets harsh and while the crowds are still thin, is the most comfortable time to take photos.

blocks.title: Dressing for the temple
blocks.html: This is an active temple, so dress modestly — skip tank tops and shorts above the knee. The grounds are wide open with almost no shade, and the midday sun is brutal, so bringing a hat and some water makes the visit far more comfortable.

blocks.text: The Hell-Heaven garden — the part everyone talks about

blocks.html: Beyond the Buddha, what makes Wat Muang memorable is the Hell-Heaven garden, an open-air statue ground that recreates the Buddhist underworld. Life-sized statues of sinners are shown being punished for their deeds — climbing the thorn tree, tormented by hungry ghosts — and some of it is rendered quite realistically and is genuinely unsettling. Small children may find it frightening, but plenty of adults see it as a vivid, hard-to-ignore lesson about sin and merit.

Walk a little further and you reach the heaven and celestial zones, with both Thai and Chinese deities, along with statues depicting Thai literature and scenes from the historic Thai–Burmese wars fought around this region. You can stroll past them in sequence like an open-air museum. Honestly, some of the statues have faded with time, but overall it's still an enjoyable spot to wander and take photos.

blocks.text: Giant lotus, glass shrine and the fish pond

items: The giant lotus-petal ordination hall — an ubosot surrounded by huge pink lotus petals. It's the photo angle you see most often in reviews, and the pink against a blue sky makes for a striking shot.

The glass shrine (Wihan Kaeo) — the lower floor holds sacred amulets and statues of several famous revered monks, while the upper floor enshrines a Sukhothai-style bhumisparsha Buddha. It's quiet and calm, a good place to sit and escape the sun.
The fish pond (Wang Macha) — a pond behind the temple where you can buy fish food for the kids. It's a favourite rest stop for families.
The Chinese deity shrine — a Chinese-style spot for prayers and blessings that adds some variety to your walk around the temple.

blocks.title: Allow enough time
blocks.html: A lot of people assume they'll just stop for a quick photo of the Buddha and leave, but if you want to walk the whole hell garden, the lotus hall, the glass shrine and the fish pond, allow around 1.5–2 hours.

Wat Muang is free to enter — there's no admission fee. It's open daily from around 06:00 to 18:00, while the indoor shrine and museum zones usually open from late morning until evening. The best times to visit are before 10:00 or after 15:00, when the sun is gentler and there are fewer people than at midday. Long weekends and Buddhist holy days get especially busy.

items: Entry fee: free (donation boxes are available if you wish to give)
Best time: before 10:00 or after 15:00 to avoid the midday heat
Parking: a large lot that handles both cars and tour buses

blocks.html: Wat Muang is about 100–110 km from Bangkok, roughly a 1.5–2 hour drive, making it an easy day trip.

items.name: Driving yourself
items.blurb: From Bangkok, take the Asia Highway (Route 32) toward Ayutthaya and Ang Thong, then turn onto Route 3195, the Ang Thong–Wiset Chai Chan road. It's well signposted, and driving is the most convenient option since you can carry on to other temples in the province afterwards.

items.name: Van / coach
items.blurb: Take a van or coach from Mo Chit to Ang Thong, around 2–2.5 hours, then catch local transport in town out to the temple.

items.name: Hiring local transport
items.blurb: From Ang Thong town, hire a tuk-tuk or local car for a round trip to Wat Muang and arrange for the driver to wait or come back for you. Including waiting time of around 2–3 hours, it shouldn't run more than a low four figures in THB.

blocks.title: Make the trip count
blocks.html: Once you're in Ang Thong, it's worth carrying on to Wat Khun Inthapramun (home to a huge reclining Buddha) and the Ekarat drum-making village, so you see a side of Ang Thong beyond just the big Buddha.

blocks.text: A one-day Ang Thong trip starting at Wat Muang

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Big temples + craft villages + Ang Thong eats

items.activity: Leave Bangkok, head up Route 32 toward Ang Thong
items.note: Set off early to dodge traffic and the midday heat

items.activity: Arrive at Wat Muang, pay respects to Luang Pho Yai, then walk the hell-heaven garden, giant lotus and glass shrine
items.note: Allow 1.5–2 hours and photograph the Buddha before the sun gets harsh

items.activity: Lunch in Ang Thong town — try boat noodles or a riverside restaurant
items.note: Ang Thong is known for boat noodles and river fish and prawns

items.activity: Stop at Wat Khun Inthapramun to see the huge reclining Buddha
items.note: It's over in Pho Thong district, not far on from town

items.activity: Visit the Ekarat drum-making village to watch the drum makers and pick up souvenirs
items.note: A craft that's a signature of Ang Thong

items.activity: Relax at a riverside cafe or grab some local sweets before heading back
items.note: Drive back to Bangkok and arrive around dusk

blocks.html: This plan works comfortably in a single day because the distances within the province are short. If you'd rather take it slow, it's easy to stay one night and extend the trip on to nearby Sing Buri or Ayutthaya.

faq.q: Is Wat Muang free to enter, and what are the hours?
faq.a: Entry is free — there's no admission fee, just donation boxes if you'd like to give. It's open daily from around 06:00 to 18:00, with the indoor shrine and museum zones usually open from late morning until evening. Come before 10:00 or after 15:00 to avoid the heat and the crowds.

faq.q: How tall is the big Buddha at Wat Muang?
faq.a: Luang Pho Yai, or Phra Phuttha Maha Nawamin Sakayamuni Si Wiset Chai Chan, is a golden seated Buddha in the bhumisparsha posture, with a lap width of around 63 metres and a height of around 95 metres. It's the largest seated Buddha image in Thailand and is visible from the road long before you reach the temple.

faq.q: How do I get to Wat Muang from Bangkok?
faq.a: It's about 100–110 km away, a 1.5–2 hour drive. Take the Asia Highway (Route 32), then turn onto Route 3195. If you don't have your own car, take a van or coach from Mo Chit to Ang Thong, around 2–2.5 hours, then catch local transport or hire a tuk-tuk in town out to the temple.

faq.q: Is the hell garden at Wat Muang scary? Can kids go?
faq.a: The hell garden is a statue ground depicting sinners being punished, and some of it is realistic and genuinely frightening. Small children may be startled, but many families bring kids to teach them about sin and merit. Further along there's a heaven and celestial zone with a more relaxed atmosphere.

faq.q: Where else can I go near Wat Muang?
faq.a: In the same province you can carry on to Wat Khun Inthapramun (with its huge reclining Buddha), the Ekarat drum-making village, and the markets and riverside spots in town. With extra time, you can extend the trip to nearby Sing Buri or Ayutthaya.
